title: Boss: the on-sale postmortem
summary: A ticket on-sale oversold 312 seats. Work through the postmortem like the reviewer: time to mitigate, which orders to refund, and the admission rate that would have kept the database calm. Then build the capstone.

steps.title: The artefact: a postmortem timeline
body: **Postmortem: winter tour on-sale (blameless).** Impact: 312 seats sold twice; about 9 minutes of degraded
booking. The timeline, from the incident channel and the dashboards:
19:07:55 fix deployed: conditional update on hold
Root cause (from the code review): the hold was a check-then-act race, and load made the window between the
read and the write long enough to matter. Contributing factor: the admission rate was set without measuring
how many bookings per second the database could confirm.
Each step below is one number the review needs. The last step builds the capstone design on the board.

steps.title: Time between two events
prompt: Write `int SecondsBetween(string[] timeline, string fromPrefix, string toPrefix)`.
- Each line is `HH:MM:SS text` (the time, one space, the text).
- Find the **first** line whose text starts with `fromPrefix`, and the first line **after** it whose text starts
with `toPrefix`. Return the seconds between their times.
- If either is missing, return `-1`.
The review's headline number is the time from detection to mitigation.
starter: int SecondsBetween(string[] timeline, string fromPrefix, string toPrefix)
solution: int SecondsBetween(string[] timeline, string fromPrefix, string toPrefix)
hints: `TimeSpan.Parse(line[..8])` reads `19:00:41`; the text starts at index 9.
Remember the `from` time once found, then keep scanning for the `to` line.
template: "19:07:55 fix deployed: conditional update on hold",
Dojo.Eq("detection to mitigation", 439, SecondsBetween(dojoT, "oversell detected", "oversell stopped"));
Dojo.Eq("sale start to detection", 41, SecondsBetween(dojoT, "sale started", "oversell detected"));
Dojo.Eq("queue open to the first sign of overload", 34, SecondsBetween(dojoT, "waiting room", "seat service"));
Dojo.Eq("the to-line must come after the from-line", -1, SecondsBetween(dojoT, "oversell stopped", "sale started"));

steps.title: Which orders to refund
prompt: Write `List<string> OrdersToRefund(List<(string Order, string Seat, int Ts)> orders)`.
The policy agreed in the review: for each seat, the **earliest** order keeps it (smallest `Ts`; if two are equal,
the smaller order id in ordinal order). Every other order for that seat is refunded.
Return the refunded order ids sorted in ordinal order.
starter: List<string> OrdersToRefund(List<(string Order, string Seat, int Ts)> orders)
solution: List<string> OrdersToRefund(List<(string Order, string Seat, int Ts)> orders) =>
hints: Group by seat. In each group, sort by `Ts` then by order id, and skip the first.
Collect the rest and sort them with `StringComparer.Ordinal`.
template: var dojoO = new List<(string, string, int)> {
Dojo.Eq("refund everyone but the first buyer of each seat", new List<string> { "o-104", "o-109", "o-110" }, OrdersToRefund(dojoO));
Dojo.Eq("seats sold once need no refund", new List<string>(), OrdersToRefund(new List<(string, string, int)> { ("o-1", "B1", 5), ("o-2", "B2", 5) }));
Dojo.Eq("no orders", new List<string>(), OrdersToRefund(new List<(string, string, int)>()));

steps.title: The admission rate the database can take
prompt: The action items ask for the waiting room to admit fans at a rate derived from the database, not a guess.
- `int AdmitPerSecond(int confirmsPerSecond, double buyRate)`: fans admitted per second so that the bookings they
make (`admitted x buyRate`) do not exceed what the database can confirm. Round **down**. A `buyRate` of `0` or
less, or above `1`, throws `ArgumentOutOfRangeException`.
- `int SecondsToSellOut(int seats, int seatsPerBooking, int confirmsPerSecond)`: bookings needed (seats divided by
seats per booking, rounded **up**), divided by the confirm rate, rounded **up**.
If the database confirms 600 bookings a second and 30% of admitted fans buy, admit 2,000 a second and the
50,000 seats (2 per booking) sell out in 42 seconds.
starter: int SecondsToSellOut(int seats, int seatsPerBooking, int confirmsPerSecond)
solution: int SecondsToSellOut(int seats, int seatsPerBooking, int confirmsPerSecond)
hints: Admitted x buyRate <= confirms, so admitted <= confirms / buyRate.
Round up with integers: `(a + b - 1) / b`.
template: Dojo.Eq("600 confirms/s at a 30% buy rate", 2000, AdmitPerSecond(600, 0.3));
Dojo.Throws<ArgumentOutOfRangeException>("a buy rate of 0 makes no sense", () => AdmitPerSecond(300, 0));
Dojo.Eq("an odd seat still needs a booking", 4, SecondsToSellOut(7, 2, 1));

steps.title: Capstone: design photo sharing
prompt: Put the whole topic together. In the **System design board**, start from nothing but the users and design a
photo-sharing service: uploads go straight to object storage with presigned URLs, views come from a CDN and a
cache, everything survives losing an availability zone, and it all fits the budget. The board's load test checks
every goal.
steps.explain: This is the interview answer made real: estimates told you bytes dominate, so the bytes never touch your servers; reads are skewed, so caches and the CDN carry them; and N+1 headroom across zones keeps the SLO through a failure.
